reviews.notes: The inverted Ashvattha tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are Vedic hymns; he who knows it is the Veda-knower.
Its branches spread above and below nourished by Gunas with sense objects as buds; secondary roots stretch downward binding man to action; includes footnote 30.
Its true form is not perceived here, nor its end, beginning, or foundation; cutting down this firmly rooted Ashvattha with the strong weapon of detachment; ends at '--to set'.
Then that goal must be sought from which none return: 'I take refuge in that Primal Person whence streamed forth ancient cosmic activity'; starts at 'New growths'.
Free from pride and delusion, victorious over the evil of attachment, constant in spiritual knowledge, freed from dualities of pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach the eternal goal.
Neither sun, nor moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, having reached which souls do not return.
An eternal fraction of Myself in the world of the living, becoming a living soul, draws to itself the five senses and mind seated in Prakriti.
When the Lord acquires a body and when He leaves it, He takes these senses and mind along as the wind carries scents from flower-beds.
Presiding over ear, eye, touch, taste, smell, and mind, the soul experiences the objects of the senses.
The deluded do not perceive the soul departing, staying, or experiencing united with the Gunas; those with eyes of wisdom see.
Striving yogis perceive Him established in themselves; but the unrefined and unintelligent, though striving, do not perceive Him.
The radiance in the sun illuminating the entire universe, in the moon, and in fire—know that splendor to be Mine.
Entering the earth I sustain all beings with My vital force, and becoming the sapful moon I nourish all plants.
Becoming the Vaishvanara digestive fire in living bodies, uniting with prana and apana, I digest the four kinds of food; ends with note 31 marker.
Verified source omission. Arnold explicitly omits canonical 15.15 ('sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo...'), confirmed by footnote 31 ('I omit a verse here, evidently interpolated.').
Two persons in the world: the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the immutable/kutastha).
The Supreme Person is another, declared as Paramatman, the imperishable Lord Who enters the three worlds and sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and the Vedas as Purushottama.
He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the Purushottama, knows all and worships Me with his whole being.
Thus this most secret doctrine has been imparted by Me; knowing this, a man becomes truly wise and fulfills all duties.

chapterFindings: Arnold translates verses 15.1–15.6 in lyrical rhymed stanzas ('Parable of the fig-tree', note 30), requiring careful inter-stanza clause alignment across enjambments.
Verse 15.15 is an explicit, verified source omission where Arnold dropped the shloka on memory, knowledge, and Vedic authorship, directly attested by footnote 31.
The remaining 19 verses map with exceptional precision to canonical 15.1–15.14 and 15.16–15.20.
